kw: The process of being made holy. It appears three times in vv. 3–7: holiness is God's will, God's call and God's work in us.

In v. 4 Paul literally says “to possess his own vessel”. Some Fathers and modern scholars take it as one's own body (so the NRSV: “control your own body”); others as one's wife. Either way the point is self-mastery and respect.
vv: For this is the will of God, your sanctification:
People often ask what God's will is for their lives. Paul answers first not with a job or a place, but with holiness.
For God did not call us to impurity but in holiness.
Therefore whoever rejects this rejects not human authority but God, who also gives his Holy Spirit to you.
Christian chastity is not a human rule imposed from outside. The body of the baptised is a dwelling of the Holy Spirit (compare 1 Corinthians 6:19).
ch: The Second Vatican Council quotes 1 Thessalonians 4:3 when it teaches that all the faithful, in every state of life, are called to holiness (Lumen Gentium 39–40). The Catechism describes chastity as the successful integration of sexuality within the person, a work of grace and of daily effort (CCC 2337–2338).

r.h: The Beatitudes
set: The Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7) is the first of five great discourses in Matthew. Jesus goes up the mountain and sits down to teach, as a rabbi did, and the scene recalls Moses on Sinai. But Jesus does not bring a law carved on stone; he begins with a blessing.
str: vv. 1–2: the setting: the mountain, the crowds, the disciples.
vv. 3–10: eight beatitudes. The first and the eighth end with the same promise, “theirs is the kingdom of heaven”, framing the whole.
vv. 11–12: a ninth beatitude, now spoken directly to the disciples: “Blessed are you”.
kw: Not a wish but a declaration, like the Hebrew ’ašrê of the Psalms (“Happy are those”, Psalm 1:1). Jesus announces who is already blessed in God's eyes.
The ‘ănāwîm of the Old Testament: the lowly who have nothing to rely on but God. It is not a love of misery but a total dependence on the Father.
Gentle strength, not weakness. The promise echoes Psalm 37:11, “the meek shall inherit the land”. Jesus calls himself “gentle and humble in heart” (11:29).
vv: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
The first beatitude is the door to all the others. Only empty hands can receive.
Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.
In the Bible the heart is the centre of thinking and choosing. A pure heart is undivided, and so it can see. This beatitude is the Gospel's answer to the epistle's call to holiness.
Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God.
ch: The Catechism says that the Beatitudes depict the face of Jesus Christ and portray his charity (CCC 1717); they are first a portrait of him, and then a path for us. St Augustine, in his commentary on the Sermon on the Mount, linked the Beatitudes with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit named in Isaiah 11, as steps of a ladder from humility to wisdom (in substance).

qa: Are the Beatitudes commands or promises?
Both. They are first good news: God's blessing on the lowly. But they also describe the way of life of those who follow Jesus, and so they call us to become what they describe (CCC 1716–1717).
study: Paul says God's will is “your sanctification”. What is one concrete step of holiness God is asking of me this week?
Which beatitude do I find hardest to accept as a blessing, and why?

lead: Today the Church remembers the 318 Fathers of the Council of Nicaea, and the readings fit the day. Hebrews tells us to remember the leaders who spoke God's word to us and to imitate their faith, because “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” In the Gospel, the faithful servant is the one who feeds the household at the proper time, until the master comes.

r.h: Remember your leaders; Christ does not change
set: Chapter 13 closes the long sermon of Hebrews with practical counsel: love, hospitality, marriage, money, and the community's leaders. The “leaders” of v. 7 seem to be those who first preached to them and have already died, perhaps as martyrs, since the readers are told to consider “the outcome” of their life. The living leaders are mentioned in v. 17.
str: vv. 7–8: remember your leaders; Christ is unchanging.
vv. 9–10: do not be carried away by strange teachings; “we have an altar”.
vv. 11–14: as the sin offerings were burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27), Jesus suffered outside the city gate; let us go out to him.
vv. 15–16: the sacrifices Christians offer: praise, doing good, sharing.
kw: Those who guide and go ahead. The same word is used for the leaders who are still alive in vv. 17 and 24.
“We have an altar” (v. 10). Many interpreters see here the cross of Christ; Catholic tradition has also seen the Eucharistic table, where we eat of the one sacrifice.
An Old Testament phrase (Psalm 50:14, 23 in the Greek). Hebrews adds “the fruit of lips” from Hosea 14:2.
vv: Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith.
Christians are asked not only to remember their teachers but to look at how their lives ended, and to copy their faith, not merely their words.
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
Leaders pass; Christ remains. This is why the faith confessed at Nicaea is still our faith: it is faith in the same Christ.
Let us then go to him outside the camp and bear the abuse he endured.
ch: The Catechism lists “the sacrifice of praise” (Hebrews 13:15) among the names of the Eucharist, which makes present the one sacrifice of Christ (CCC 1330). It also teaches that the bishops, as successors of the apostles, hand on the faith received, so that the Church remains in the teaching of the apostles (CCC 77, 857).

r.h: The faithful and wise servant
set: This short parable belongs to Jesus' last discourse about the end of the age (Matthew 24–25). The question is not when the master will come, but what he will find his servant doing when he comes. Luke has the same parable and adds that Peter asked, “Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for everyone?” (Luke 12:41).
str: v. 45: the question: who is the faithful and wise servant?
vv. 46–47: the blessing of the one found at work.
vv. 48–49: the wicked servant who says, “My master is delayed.”
vv. 50–51: the master's sudden coming and the servant's ruin.
kw: Faithful toward the master, wise in caring for the household. The same word “wise” describes the wise bridesmaids (25:2) and the man who built on rock (7:24).
The servant's mistake is to treat delay as absence. The Lord's patience is not a sign that he will not come.
A deliberately shocking image of total punishment, which many scholars take as “cut off” from the household. The point is the seriousness of a trust betrayed.
vv: Who then is the faithful and wise slave, whom his master has put in charge of his household, to give the other slaves their allowance of food at the proper time?
The servant is a servant among servants. Authority in the household is for feeding others, not for ruling them.
Blessed is that slave whom his master will find at work when he arrives.
But if that wicked slave says to himself, ‘My master is delayed,’
The fall begins in the heart, with a private sentence: there is plenty of time. Then come violence toward others and self-indulgence (v. 49).
ch: The Church reads this parable first for her pastors, and then for every Christian who has been given others to care for. The Catechism teaches that ministry in the Church is service: those who receive it become “slaves of Christ” for the sake of the people (CCC 876). It also recalls the Council's call to watch constantly, since we know neither the day nor the hour (CCC 1036; Lumen Gentium 48).

qa: Who were the 318 Fathers?

The bishops who met at Nicaea in AD 325, the first ecumenical council, and confessed that the Son is “one in being with the Father” against the teaching of Arius. The number 318 is the traditional count; St Ambrose noted that it is also the number of Abraham's servants in Genesis 14:14 (in substance). Their Creed, completed at Constantinople in 381, is the one we profess today.
rite: In the Holy Qurbono the Malankara Church professes the Nicene Creed, the faith of the 318 Fathers as completed at Constantinople. When we say “one in being with the Father”, we stand with Nicaea and with the faithful leaders whom Hebrews tells us to remember.
study: Who first spoke the word of God to me? How can I imitate their faith, and not only remember them?
In my home, parish or work, whom has the Lord put in my care “to give them their food at the proper time”?

lead: Both readings are about pride and judgment. Paul asks the Corinthians, who were proud of their gifts and of their favourite teachers, “What do you have that you did not receive?” In the Gospel, Jesus warns against judging others while blind to our own faults. Humility before God becomes mercy toward our neighbour.

r.h: What do you have that you did not receive?
set: Paul wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus, around AD 54–55. Chapters 1–4 deal with the quarrels in the church at Corinth, where groups were forming around different preachers (1:12). Some Corinthians thought of themselves as already wise, rich and spiritually complete. Paul answers with irony, and then with a father's tenderness.
str: v. 6: Paul has applied all this to himself and Apollos, so that no one may be “puffed up” for one against another.
v. 7: three questions that undo all boasting.
vv. 8–10: irony: “Already you have become rich!” set against the apostles' weakness.
vv. 11–13: the real life of an apostle: hunger, blows, manual work, blessing in return for insults.
v. 14: “not to make you ashamed, but to admonish you as my beloved children”.
kw: A word Paul uses almost only in this letter (4:6, 18, 19; 5:2; 8:1; 13:4). Knowledge “puffs up”, but love builds up (8:1).
Paul pictures the apostles as condemned prisoners brought out last in the arena, watched by the world, by angels and by people.
What is scraped off and thrown away. Paul accepts being treated as the world's rubbish for the sake of Christ.
vv: For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if it were not a gift?
Every gift, of nature or of grace, is received. Boasting forgets the Giver.
we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels and to mortals.
When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure;
Paul lives what Jesus taught: “bless those who curse you” (Luke 6:28). The apostle's authority shows itself in this kind of meekness.
ch: St Augustine said that 1 Corinthians 4:7 convinced him that even the beginning of faith is God's gift, and he quoted it again and again against the idea that we can earn grace (in substance; On the Predestination of the Saints). The Catechism teaches that before God we have no strict right to any merit: our merits are themselves God's gifts (CCC 2007–2011).

r.h: Do not judge
set: These verses belong to Luke's Sermon on the Plain (6:20–49), his shorter parallel to the Sermon on the Mount. Just before, Jesus has said: “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (6:36). Today's words show what that mercy means between people.
str: vv. 37–38: four commands with four promises: do not judge, do not condemn, forgive, give; the good measure.
vv. 39–40: the blind guide; the disciple and the teacher.
vv. 41–42: the speck and the log.
kw: Jesus does not forbid all moral discernment (compare 6:43–45 on knowing a tree by its fruit). He forbids passing sentence on people, which belongs to God.
A speck is a tiny bit of straw or chaff; a dokos is a roof beam. The comic exaggeration is meant to make us laugh, and then to see ourselves.
The fold of a long garment, pulled up and used as a pocket for grain. The measure of wheat is pressed down, shaken and overflowing: the generosity of God.
vv: Do not judge, and you will not be judged; do not condemn, and you will not be condemned. Forgive, and you will be forgiven;
The passive verbs (“will be judged”, “will be forgiven”) are a reverent way of speaking of what God will do.
for the measure you give will be the measure you get back.
Why do you see the speck in your neighbor’s eye, but do not notice the log in your own eye?
The one who judges harshly is often blind to his own faults. Correction of a brother is still possible, but only after we have dealt with ourselves (v. 42).
ch: The Catechism teaches that although we can judge that an act is in itself a grave offence, we must entrust the judgment of persons to the justice and mercy of God (CCC 1861). It also warns against rash judgment and asks us to interpret our neighbour's words and deeds in a favourable way as far as possible (CCC 2477–2478).

qa: Does “Do not judge” mean we may never call anything wrong?

No. Jesus himself calls sin by its name, and the Church must teach right and wrong. What is forbidden is condemning persons, presuming to know their hearts, and correcting others while ignoring our own sins (CCC 1861, 2478).
study: Paul asks, “What do you have that you did not receive?” Name three gifts I received and have sometimes treated as my own achievement.
Whom do I find it easiest to judge? What “log” in my own eye might the Lord be showing me?

lead: Both readings speak of the Father and his children. Hebrews explains hardship as the training a loving Father gives his children, so that we may share his holiness. In John, Jesus reveals himself as the Son who does nothing on his own but only what he sees the Father doing. The Son's perfect obedience is the pattern of our sonship.

r.h: The Lord disciplines those he loves
set: After the great list of the heroes of faith (chapter 11), Hebrews pictures the Christian life as a race, run with eyes fixed on Jesus, “who for the sake of the joy that was set before him endured the cross” (12:1–2). The readers are tired and facing hostility. The author now explains their struggles by quoting Proverbs 3:11–12.
str: v. 4: you have not yet resisted to the point of blood.
vv. 5–6: the quotation from Proverbs: the Lord disciplines those he loves.
vv. 7–8: discipline is a sign that we are truly his children.
vv. 9–10: earthly fathers and “the Father of spirits”.
v. 11: painful now, fruitful later.
kw: From pais, child: the whole upbringing of a child, teaching as well as correction. The word is used eight times in these verses.
The word behind “gymnasium”. Hardship is pictured as an athlete's training, not as a punishment for its own sake.
The goal of the Father's training is that “we may share his holiness” (v. 10): not only good behaviour, but a share in God's own life.
vv: for the Lord disciplines those whom he loves, and chastises every child whom he accepts.
Hebrews does not say that every suffering is sent as a punishment. It says that a believer can receive even hardship from the hands of a Father who loves.
but he disciplines us for our good, in order that we may share his holiness.
Now, discipline always seems painful rather than pleasant at the time, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.
An honest verse: it does not pretend that pain is pleasant. The fruit comes “later”, and it is peace.
ch: The Church teaches that suffering, accepted in union with Christ, takes on a new meaning and becomes a share in his saving work (CCC 1521). St John Paul II, in his letter Salvifici Doloris, speaks of suffering as a call to conversion and to growth in goodness, and above all as a way of sharing in the sufferings of Christ (in substance).

r.h: The Son does what he sees the Father doing
set: Jesus has healed a man at the pool of Bethesda on the sabbath (5:1–18). Some of the authorities in Jerusalem objected, and John says they sought to kill him because he was “calling God his own Father, thereby making himself equal to God” (5:18). Jesus answers in a long discourse (5:19–47), of which these verses are the opening.
str: v. 19: the Son does nothing on his own, only what he sees the Father doing.
v. 20: the Father loves the Son and shows him everything.
v. 21: as the Father raises the dead, so the Son gives life.
v. 22: all judgment is given to the Son.
v. 23: so that all may honour the Son as they honour the Father.
¶ Many scholars hear behind v. 19 a small picture from daily life: an apprentice son who learns his father's trade by watching him at work and doing the same.
kw: A solemn opening found only in John, always on the lips of Jesus. It marks what follows as weighty.
The power to give life belongs to God alone. Jesus claims it for himself, both now (5:24) and at the resurrection of the dead (5:28–29).
The Greek word means both judgment and decision. In John, judgment happens already as people accept or refuse the Son (3:18–19).
vv: Very truly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing on his own, but only what he sees the Father doing; for whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise.
This is not weakness but perfect unity. The Son acts as the Father acts, because he is from the Father and one with him.
just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes.
so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.
The same honour for the Son as for the Father: this is the faith that the Council of Nicaea later put into the words “one in being with the Father”.
ch: The Catechism teaches that full right to pass definitive judgment belongs to Christ as Redeemer, and cites John 5:22 (CCC 679). St Augustine, preaching on these verses, explains that the Son's “seeing” the Father is not like our seeing: for the Son, to see is to be born of the Father, and so to be equal with him (in substance; Tractates on John).

qa: If the Son “can do nothing on his own”, is he less than the Father?

No. The verse speaks of unity, not of inferiority: the Son never acts apart from the Father, and “whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise”. Verse 23 asks for equal honour for both. The Church confesses the Son as true God, one in being with the Father (CCC 242).
study: Is there a hardship in my life that I could begin to receive as the training of a loving Father?
Jesus does what he sees the Father doing. What do I “see” of the Father in prayer that I could do today?

lead: Today's readings set two kinds of wealth side by side. Paul tells Timothy to warn the rich not to trust in uncertain riches but to be “rich in good works”. In the Gospel, a woman known as a sinner pours out costly ointment and tears on the feet of Jesus, and is called rich in love. The true treasure is a heart that has received much and gives much.

r.h: Rich in good works
set: 1 Timothy is one of the three Pastoral Letters, addressed to Timothy, Paul's companion, who was caring for the church at Ephesus. Earlier in this chapter the letter warns that “the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil” (6:10). Now, near the end, it turns to those in the community who are already rich, and does not condemn them but gives them a task.
str: v. 17: two warnings (do not be haughty; do not hope in riches) and the right hope: God, who richly provides.
v. 18: four positive commands: do good, be rich in good works, be generous, share.
v. 19: the result: a good foundation for the future, and “the life that really is life”.
kw: The letter speaks of the rich “in the present age”: their riches belong to a world that is passing.
From koinōnia, communion. Sharing goods is a form of the fellowship of the Church (compare Acts 2:44–45).
the life that really is life
Literally “the real life”. Wealth gives a kind of life; God gives the life that is truly life.
vv: As for those who in the present age are rich, command them not to be haughty, or to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but rather on God who richly provides us with everything for our enjoyment.
Notice the last words: God gives us things “for our enjoyment”. The letter does not despise created goods; it puts them in their place.
They are to do good, to be rich in good works, generous, and ready to share,
so that they may take hold of the life that really is life.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the owner of goods is a steward of Providence, who should make them bear fruit and share the benefits with others, first of all his family (CCC 2404). It quotes St John Chrysostom: “Not to enable the poor to share in our goods is to steal from them and deprive them of life” (CCC 2446).

r.h: The woman who loved much
set: This scene is found only in Luke. Jesus has just been called “a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (7:34), and now we see what that means. A Pharisee named Simon invites him to a meal. Luke shows Jesus at table with Pharisees several times (11:37; 14:1), and the meal becomes a lesson for the host.
str: vv. 36–38: the woman's act at Jesus' feet.
v. 39: Simon's silent judgment.
vv. 40–43: the parable of two debtors.
vv. 44–46: three contrasts: water, kiss, oil.
v. 47: her many sins forgiven; little forgiveness, little love.
vv. 48–50: “Your sins are forgiven … Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”
kw: Luke does not tell us her sin, and he does not give her a name. She is known by her love.
A labourer's wage for one day (Matthew 20:2). The two debts are about a year and a half's wages, and less than two months'.

The little word hoti can give the reason (“because”) or the evidence (“which shows that”). The NRSV reads “hence she has shown great love”, following the parable, where love comes from forgiveness; the Malayalam POC reads “because she loved much”. Catholic interpreters hold both: love is the fruit of forgiveness received, and love opens the heart to receive it.
vv: She stood behind him at his feet, weeping, and began to bathe his feet with her tears and to dry them with her hair.
Guests reclined on low couches with their feet stretched out behind them, so she could reach his feet without coming to the table. Every gesture is a gesture of love: tears, hair, kisses, ointment.
Do you see this woman?
Simon has seen only “a sinner” (v. 39). Jesus asks him to see a person.
Therefore, I tell you, her sins, which were many, have been forgiven; hence she has shown great love. But the one to whom little is forgiven, loves little.
Your faith has saved you; go in peace.
The same words Jesus speaks to the woman healed of bleeding (8:48). Faith receives; peace is the gift.
ch: The Catechism teaches that only God forgives sins, and that Jesus, as Son of God, exercises this divine power and gives it to his Church (CCC 1441–1442). The guests' question, “Who is this who even forgives sins?” (v. 49), is the right question. Pope St Gregory the Great, preaching on this Gospel, saw in the woman's tears the model of a penitent who turns all that once served sin into the service of God (in substance).

qa: Was this woman Mary Magdalene?

Luke does not say so. He introduces Mary Magdalene separately in the next chapter (8:2). In the West, from the time of St Gregory the Great, the two were often identified; the Eastern tradition has generally kept them distinct. The Church does not require either view; the Gospel's point is her love and her forgiveness.
study: Paul tells the rich to be “rich in good works”. What could I share this week, of money, time or skill?
Simon saw “a sinner”; Jesus saw a woman who loved. Whom do I need to see with the eyes of Jesus?

lead: Today the Church remembers the 33 Martyrs of Melitene, soldiers honoured in the Eastern calendars, of whom little is known for certain. The readings ask what people see when they look at the Church. Paul pleads with the Corinthians to stop dividing into parties, because Christ is not divided. In the Gospel, some Greeks come with a request every parish should hear: “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.”

r.h: Is Christ divided?
set: Right after his opening thanksgiving, Paul goes straight to the first problem at Corinth: quarrels. People from the household of Chloe have told him that the community is splitting into groups around favourite preachers. Paul had founded the church; Apollos, an eloquent teacher from Alexandria, had worked there after him (Acts 18:24–28); some may have known Peter, or claimed his authority.
str: v. 10: the appeal: no divisions, the same mind and purpose.
vv. 11–12: the report and the four slogans.
v. 13: three questions: Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Were you baptised in Paul's name?
vv. 14–16: Paul is glad he baptised few of them.
v. 17: his mission: to preach the gospel, so that the cross is not emptied of its power.
kw: Literally “tears”, as in a torn garment (the same word in Mark 2:21). From it comes our word “schism”.
The word used for mending fishing nets (Mark 1:19). Unity is something to be repaired with patience.
If the gospel depends on the preacher's cleverness, the cross is “emptied” of its power. The power is in Christ crucified, not in the messenger.
vv: Now I appeal to you, brothers and sisters, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you be in agreement and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be united in the same mind and the same purpose.
Has Christ been divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?
Three questions with one obvious answer. Christians belong to Christ, who was crucified for them, and into whose name they were baptised.
For Christ did not send me to baptize but to proclaim the gospel, and not with eloquent wisdom, so that the cross of Christ might not be emptied of its power.
Paul is not belittling baptism, which he himself administered (vv. 14–16). He is saying that his particular mission was preaching, and that no minister should become the centre.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that division among Christians openly contradicts the will of Christ, scandalises the world and damages the preaching of the Gospel (Unitatis Redintegratio 1). The Catechism speaks of the wounds to the unity of the Church and of the call to pray and work for the unity of all Christians (CCC 817–822).

r.h: Sir, we wish to see Jesus
set: It is the last Passover of Jesus' ministry. He has just entered Jerusalem to the crowd's acclaim, and the Pharisees say, “Look, the world has gone after him!” (12:19). At once John shows “the world” arriving: some Greeks, probably Gentiles who worshipped the God of Israel, come up for the feast. Their coming leads Jesus to say, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified” (12:23).
str: v. 20: Greeks among the pilgrims.
v. 21: they approach Philip: “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.”
v. 22: Philip tells Andrew, and both tell Jesus.
kw: Not Greek-speaking Jews but Gentiles. In John, their arrival is a sign that Jesus will draw “all people” to himself (12:32).
In John, “seeing” Jesus often means coming to faith. Philip himself had once said, “Come and see” (1:46).
A polite address, but in John the word keeps growing in meaning until Thomas says, “My Lord and my God!” (20:28).
vv: They came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and said to him, “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.”
Philip and Andrew both have Greek names and come from Bethsaida (1:44), a town in a mixed region. Perhaps that is why the Greeks come to them.
Philip went and told Andrew; then Andrew and Philip went and told Jesus.
The disciples do not keep the seekers for themselves; they bring them to Jesus. Andrew has done this before: he brought his brother Simon (1:41–42) and the boy with the loaves (6:8–9).
ch: The coming of the Greeks shows that the Kingdom is meant for all nations: first announced to Israel, it is open to people of every people (CCC 543). In some churches these words, “Sir, we wish to see Jesus”, are written inside the pulpit where only the preacher can read them, as a reminder of what the people have come for.

qa: Why does John not tell us whether the Greeks met Jesus?

Because the answer Jesus gives is about the cross. From now on, the nations will “see” him when he is lifted up (12:32). We too see Jesus by faith, through the word and the Holy Qurbono, and in a Church that points to him.
study: When people look at my parish, or my family, do they see our divisions or do they see Jesus?
Like Philip and Andrew, whom could I bring to Jesus this week?

lead: Hudos Eetho, the Sunday of the Renewal of the Church, follows Qudos Eetho, the Sunday of her Sanctification, at the opening of the West Syriac liturgical year. Last Sunday the Church was consecrated; today she is renewed. The readings are many, and all of them circle one place: the house of God. In the evening Gospel (Mark 11:15–17) Jesus calls the Temple “a house of prayer for all the nations”. Exodus 32 shows the people making a god they can control, and Moses standing between them and God's anger. Jeremiah 31 and Isaiah 55 promise a scattered people that God will gather them and feed them again. In Revelation 3 the risen Lord knocks at the door of a comfortable, lukewarm Church.

This study takes three of them: Solomon's prayer at the dedication of the Temple, the Letter to the Hebrews on the true sanctuary, and the Gospel of John, where Jesus cleanses the Temple and speaks of the temple of his body. The line runs from a house of stone, to a tent not made with hands, to the body of Christ, destroyed and raised. Its key words are dwelling, cleansing and renewal.

r.h: Can God dwell on the earth?
set: Solomon has finished the Temple in Jerusalem, in the tenth century BC, and the ark of the covenant has been carried into the inner sanctuary. The cloud of the Lord's glory fills the house, so that the priests cannot stand to minister (8:10–11). Then the king turns to pray. Chapter 8 is the great dedication chapter of the Old Testament: the procession of the ark (vv. 1–13), Solomon's address to the people (vv. 14–21), his long prayer (vv. 22–53), the blessing (vv. 54–61), and the sacrifices and the feast (vv. 62–66).

The books of Kings received their final form during or after the Babylonian exile, when the Temple lay in ruins. For those first readers the prayer had a sharp edge. God had never been shut inside the building, and he still hears prayer offered toward this place from a far country (8:46–50).
str: v. 22: Solomon stands before the altar and spreads out his hands to heaven, the ancient posture of prayer.
vv. 23–26: praise of the God who keeps covenant, and a plea that the promise to David be confirmed.
v. 27: the great question: will God indeed dwell on the earth?
vv. 28–30: the request that God's eyes be open toward this house, and that he hear and forgive.
¶ The prayer moves from praise, to promise, to humility, to petition. Its heart is v. 27, set between two requests: the house is real and holy, yet God is greater than it.
kw: Covenant faithfulness, love that keeps its word (v. 23). It is the love God has promised and will not take back.

“My name shall be there” (v. 29). God's name stands for God himself as he makes himself known and lets himself be called upon. His name dwells in the Temple, while he himself is in heaven. In this way the book holds together God's nearness and his greatness.
The last word of the reading (v. 30). In the Old Testament this verb always has God as its subject: only God forgives in this full sense. The Temple is, above all, a house where sins are forgiven.
vv: Then Solomon stood before the altar of the Lord in the presence of all the assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands to heaven.

The king prays as head of the assembly, standing, with open hands. The first Christians prayed in the same way, as the praying figures painted in the catacombs show. Prayer begins with open hands: we come to receive.
But will God indeed dwell on the earth? Even heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you, much less this house that I have built!

Solomon has just built the finest building Israel would ever have, and his first words over it confess its smallness. “The highest heaven” is literally “the heaven of heavens”, a Hebrew way of saying the very highest. The house does not hold God; it is the place where he chooses to meet his people. The Gospel answers Solomon's question in a way he could not have imagined: “the Word became flesh and lived among us” (John 1:14).
that your eyes may be open night and day toward this house, the place of which you said, ‘My name shall be there,’

Solomon does not ask that God live in the house, but that God look toward it. Daniel in exile prays three times a day at windows open toward Jerusalem (Daniel 6:10). The Church keeps this sense of direction: we pray toward the altar, and in the Syriac tradition toward the east, from where the Lord will come.
O hear in heaven your dwelling place; heed and forgive.

The prayer ends in forgiveness. In the verses that follow (vv. 31–53) Solomon lists the troubles that will bring people to this house: injustice, defeat, drought, famine, the foreigner who comes from afar, exile. Each time the plea returns: hear and forgive.
ch: The Catechism points to this prayer when it speaks of prayer in the time of the kings: the Temple was to be the place of Israel's prayer, and Solomon's prayer at its dedication rests on God's promise and covenant (CCC 2580, in substance). The Roman Rite also reads part of this chapter (8:22–23, 27–30) at the dedication of a church. Christians read v. 27 in the light of the Incarnation: the God whom the heavens cannot contain was carried in the womb of the Virgin Mary, as the hymns of the Churches of East and West love to sing.

r.h: Until the time comes to set things right
set: Hebrews is a sermon in writing, “a word of exhortation” (13:22), sent to Christians who were growing tired and were tempted to look back. Its author does not give his name; the Church received it with the letters of St Paul. Chapters 8–10 compare the worship of the first covenant with the one offering of Christ.

The background of chapter 9 is the Day of Atonement, Yom Kippur (Leviticus 16). Once a year the high priest went behind the curtain into the Holy of Holies with the blood of a bull and a goat, and sprinkled the mercy seat for his own sins and for the sins of the people. The author describes not the Temple of his own day but the tent of the desert, as the Book of Exodus describes it.
str: vv. 1–5: the two rooms of the tent and their furnishings.
vv. 6–7: the priests enter the first room daily; the high priest alone enters the second, once a year.
vv. 8–10: what the Holy Spirit teaches by this arrangement: the way into the sanctuary was not yet open.
vv. 11–12: Christ enters the true sanctuary with his own blood.
vv. 13–14: if the blood of animals cleansed the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ cleanse the conscience.
kw: “Until the time comes to set things right” (v. 10). The word means to straighten what is crooked, to restore. The Malayalam POC renders it “the time of renewal” (നവീകരണകാലം), a fitting word for Hudos Eetho. For Hebrews, that time has come in Christ.
The inner self that knows itself guilty or clean. The old offerings “cannot perfect the conscience of the worshiper” (v. 9); the blood of Christ can (v. 14). Renewal in Hebrews begins inside.
Works that come from sin and lead to death. Some also hear in the phrase the old rites, which could not give life. From these the conscience is cleansed, so that it may worship.
vv: By this the Holy Spirit indicates that the way into the sanctuary has not yet been disclosed as long as the first tent is still standing.

The arrangement of the tent was itself a lesson. A curtain, and a single entry once a year, said plainly that the way was still closed. When Jesus died, “the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom” (Mark 15:38), and the way was opened.
he entered once for all into the Holy Place, not with the blood of goats and calves, but with his own blood, thus obtaining eternal redemption.

Once for all: the high priest had to return every year; Christ does not. In v. 11 the manuscripts differ between “the good things that have come” (NRSV) and “the good things to come” (POC). Both are true of Christ.
how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to worship the living God!

The verse ends not with forgiveness alone but with worship. We are cleansed in order to serve the living God, and the verb is the word for liturgical service. The goal of redemption is a worshipping people.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ, the one high priest, entered once for all into the heavenly sanctuary (CCC 662), and that the Eucharist is the memorial which makes present his one sacrifice (CCC 1364–1366). The Second Vatican Council says that the Church, holding sinners in her bosom, is at once holy and always in need of being purified, and follows constantly the path of penance and renewal (Lumen Gentium 8). Hebrews shows where that renewal comes from: not first from new plans, but from the blood of Christ, which cleanses the conscience and makes us able to worship.

r.h: The temple of his body
set: John places this scene at the beginning of Jesus' public life, at the first of the three Passovers his Gospel mentions (2:13; 6:4; 11:55). Matthew, Mark and Luke tell it in the last week, after the entry into Jerusalem; this evening's Gospel from Mark is that account. Whatever the order of events, John has set it at the start as a sign that explains his whole Gospel: Jesus himself is the new Temple.

Pilgrims coming for Passover needed animals without blemish for sacrifice, and the Temple tax was paid in Tyrian silver coins, so money changers sat in the outer court. The trade was lawful and useful. Jesus' action is a prophetic sign, like the signs of Jeremiah, against worship turned into a market.
str: vv. 13–14: Passover, Jerusalem, and the trade in the Temple courts.
vv. 15–16: the whip of cords, the overturned tables, and the word about his Father's house.
v. 17: the disciples remember Psalm 69.
vv. 18–20: the authorities ask for a sign; Jesus answers with the riddle of the temple destroyed and raised.
vv. 21–22: the evangelist explains: he spoke of his body, and the disciples understood after the Resurrection.
kw: In vv. 14–15 John uses hieron, the whole Temple area with its courts, where the trading took place. In vv. 19–21 he uses naos, the sanctuary itself, the dwelling of God. The body of Jesus is the naos, the true dwelling of God among us.

Burning, jealous love. Psalm 69 says that zeal for God's house “has consumed me”, in the past; John writes “will consume me”, in the future. The disciples see the Passion in it: Jesus' love for his Father's house will cost him his life.
Zechariah ends his prophecy with the day when “there shall no longer be traders in the house of the Lord of hosts” (Zechariah 14:21). Jesus acts as the one who brings that day.
vv: Making a whip of cords, he drove all of them out of the temple, both the sheep and the cattle.
Only John mentions the whip, and the sentence suggests that it was used to drive out the sheep and the cattle. The scene shows authority, not cruelty.
Stop making my Father’s house a marketplace!
In his first scene in Jerusalem Jesus calls God “my Father”. The Temple is his Father's home, and he speaks as the Son of the house.
Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.

The command is ironic. Others will destroy the temple of his body, and he will raise it. At his trial the saying was twisted against him (Mark 14:58). The verb “raise up” is the verb used for the Resurrection.
This temple has been under construction for forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?

Herod the Great began rebuilding the Temple around 20/19 BC, and the work went on long after. Forty-six years points to about AD 27/28, a useful date for the start of Jesus' ministry. The Temple was finished only a few years before the Romans destroyed it in AD 70.
But he was speaking of the temple of his body.
After he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this; and they believed the scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.

Understanding comes later, in the light of Easter and through the Holy Spirit, who will “remind you of all that I have said to you” (John 14:26). The Church always reads the Scriptures from the empty tomb.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus went up to the Temple as the privileged place of meeting with God, and drove out the traders out of jealous love for his Father (CCC 584). He did not despise the Temple. He presented himself as God's definitive dwelling among us, the true Temple, whose destruction and raising would be his death and Resurrection (CCC 586, in substance). When John writes “the Jews” here, he means the Temple authorities who questioned Jesus, not the Jewish people. The Church teaches that the Jewish people as such may not be blamed for Jesus' death (CCC 597; Nostra Aetate 4).

Because the risen body of Christ is the true Temple, the Church, his Body, is also God's temple, and each believer is a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 3:16; 6:19; CCC 797). St Augustine, preaching at the dedication of a church, told his people that this building is the house of our prayers, but we ourselves are the house of God, built in this life and dedicated at the end of time (in substance). The church building is holy because it signifies and serves this living temple (CCC 1179–1180).

qa: Was Jesus angry? Is anger a sin?

Anger is a passion; it becomes sin when it seeks a wrong end or goes beyond measure. Jesus' anger is holy zeal: love for his Father's house, and for the nations who came to pray there (Mark 11:17). St Paul writes, “Be angry but do not sin” (Ephesians 4:26).
If God cannot be contained in a building, why do we consecrate churches?

Solomon asked the same question. God does not need a house, but we do. A church is the visible sign of the Church, the place where the community gathers, hears the Word and celebrates the sacraments (CCC 1180–1181, in substance). It is holy not because it holds God, but because he has chosen to meet his people there.
Did Jesus cleanse the Temple once or twice?

John places it at the beginning, the other three Gospels at the end. Some interpreters think there were two cleansings; many think John set the one event at the beginning for its meaning, as a key to his whole Gospel. The Church has not decided the question, and the teaching is the same either way: Jesus is the Lord of the Temple and its fulfilment.
rite: In the West Syriac calendar the liturgical year opens with the Sundays of the Church: Qudos Eetho, when the Church is sanctified, and Hudos Eetho, when she is renewed. Before the Sundays of the Annunciations begin next week, the Church looks at herself. A church and its altar are consecrated with holy Myron, and the altar becomes the place of the Lord's presence among his people. Today's Gospel asks every parish a plain question: is our church a house of prayer, or a marketplace? The renewal that Hudos Eetho prays for begins in the heart, is fed at the altar in the Holy Qurbono, and shows itself in the life of the parish.
study: Solomon asks, “Will God indeed dwell on the earth?” How does the Incarnation answer him, and how does the Holy Qurbono?
Hebrews 9:10 speaks of “the time to set things right”. What in my life, my family or my parish most needs to be set right this year?
What “trading” has crept into the way I pray or serve in the Church?
Jesus' disciples understood his word only after the Resurrection. Which word of the Gospel have I understood only later, through experience?

lead: The week after Hudos Eetho keeps God's people on the way. Hebrews speaks of a rest that still lies ahead, and of the “today” in which we must not harden our hearts. In Matthew the Father does not want even one little one to be lost, and the shepherd goes after the one that strayed. Entering God's rest and being brought back by the shepherd are one grace seen from two sides.

r.h: A sabbath rest still remains
set: Hebrews 3–4 is a sermon on Psalm 95, the psalm that warns, “O that today you would listen to his voice!” The generation of the desert heard the good news of the promised land but did not enter, because of disobedience. The author draws the lesson for Christians: the promise is still open, and the word “today” is spoken to us.
str: vv. 6–7: the promise remains open, and God sets a new day, “today”.
v. 8: Joshua did not give the final rest.
vv. 9–10: a sabbath rest remains for God's people.
v. 11: make every effort to enter.
kw: The word Psalm 95 uses for the promised land as God's rest. Hebrews reads it as more than land: it is a share in God's own rest.
A rare word, found nowhere else in the New Testament. It means keeping sabbath: a rest that is also feast and worship, like God's rest on the seventh day (Genesis 2:2).
The key word of the passage. God's offer is always in the present tense, and every day of the Church's life is that “today”.
vv: For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not speak later about another day.
In Greek, Joshua's name is Iēsous, the same as Jesus. The first Joshua led Israel into the land; the second leads his people into God's own rest.
So then, a sabbath rest still remains for the people of God;
Let us therefore make every effort to enter that rest, so that no one may fall through such disobedience as theirs.
Rest is a gift, yet we must strive to enter it. Grace does not make us idle; it makes effort possible.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Sunday, the day of the Resurrection, fulfils the spiritual truth of the sabbath and announces our eternal rest in God (CCC 2174–2175). St Augustine ends The City of God with the great sabbath that has no evening, where we shall rest and see, see and love, love and praise (in substance).

r.h: The one that went astray
set: Matthew 18 is the fourth of Jesus' five great discourses, often called the discourse on life in the Church. It begins with the disciples asking who is the greatest, and Jesus puts a child among them. “These little ones” are the humble and weak members of the community. Luke tells the parable of the lost sheep about sinners and the joy of finding them (Luke 15:3–7); Matthew tells it about the care the Church owes to a brother or sister who strays.
str: v. 10: do not despise the little ones; their angels see the Father's face.
vv. 12–13: the shepherd, the hundred sheep, and the one that went astray.
v. 14: the Father's will: not one should be lost.

¶ The NRSV goes from v. 10 to v. 12. Verse 11, a saying that the Son of Man came to save the lost, is missing from the oldest manuscripts and was probably added from Luke 19:10. The POC numbers the verses differently and divides v. 10 into two.
kw: Not only children, but disciples who are small and vulnerable in the community.
To wander. Matthew uses the same verb for those who lead people astray (24:4–5). The sheep is not called wicked, but lost on the hills.
vv: Take care that you do not despise one of these little ones; for, I tell you, in heaven their angels continually see the face of my Father in heaven.
The little ones have friends in the highest court. From this verse the Church has learned her teaching on guardian angels.
So it is not the will of your Father in heaven that one of these little ones should be lost.
ch: The Catechism cites v. 10 when it teaches that from infancy to death human life is surrounded by the watchful care and intercession of angels (CCC 336), and v. 14 to show that God's love excludes no one (CCC 605). Many Fathers, among them St Gregory the Great, saw in the shepherd Christ himself, who left heaven to seek the lost human race (in substance).

qa: Does each person have a guardian angel?
Yes. The Catechism quotes St Basil: beside each believer stands an angel as protector and shepherd, leading him to life (CCC 336).
study: Where is “today” in my life, the moment when I must not harden my heart?
Who are the “little ones” in my parish or family whom I may be overlooking?

lead: Two readings about work and reward. Paul tells Christian slaves to serve well, so that the name of God is not blasphemed. Jesus tells of an owner who pays the last as he pays the first. In both, the measure is not our own claim but God's goodness and the honour of his name.

r.h: So that the name of God may not be blasphemed
set: The Pastoral Letters (1 and 2 Timothy, Titus) give Timothy, Paul's coworker, instructions for ordering the church at Ephesus. Here they speak to Christians who were slaves, a large part of the early communities. Slavery was a legal institution of the Roman world; the letter does not treat it as a law to reform, but speaks to believers living inside it.

The New Testament had already planted the seed that would undo slavery: in Christ “there is no longer slave or free” (Galatians 3:28), and Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus “no longer as a slave but more than a slave, a beloved brother” (Philemon 16). The Church today teaches without hesitation that slavery is an offence against human dignity (Gaudium et Spes 27; CCC 2414).
str: v. 1: slaves of unbelieving masters: honour them, so that God's name and the teaching are not blasphemed.
v. 2a: slaves of believing masters: do not despise them because they are brothers; serve them all the more.
v. 2b: “Teach and urge these duties.”
kw: The concern is mission: outsiders judge the Gospel by the conduct of Christians.
Master and slave are brothers in the Church. This word, more than any law, began to change the relationship from within.
vv: Let all who are under the yoke of slavery regard their masters as worthy of all honor, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be blasphemed.
rather they must serve them all the more, since those who benefit by their service are believers and beloved.
Belonging to the same Church does not cancel daily duties; it deepens them. Faith shows itself first at work.
ch: The Church reads these verses as a lesson for all work: to serve honestly and well, as for the Lord, is a witness to the Gospel. Human work can be a means of sanctification (CCC 2427), while every form of enslaving human beings is firmly condemned (CCC 2414).

r.h: The laborers in the vineyard
set: The parable is found only in Matthew. It follows Peter's question, “Look, we have left everything and followed you. What then will we have?” (19:27), and Jesus' saying that many who are first will be last (19:30). The parable ends with the same saying turned around (20:16).

A denarius was the usual daily wage of a laborer. Day laborers waited in the marketplace to be hired, and the Law required that they be paid each day before sunset (Deuteronomy 24:15). The day was counted from about six in the morning, so the third, sixth, ninth and eleventh hours become, in the NRSV, nine o'clock, noon, three and five.
str: vv. 1–7: the owner goes out five times to hire laborers.
vv. 8–10: payment begins with the last; all receive a denarius.
vv. 11–12: the first grumble.
vv. 13–15: the owner's answer.
v. 16: the last will be first.
kw: A polite but distant form of address. Matthew uses it three times: here, to the guest without a wedding robe (22:12), and to Judas in the garden (26:50).
“Are you envious because I am generous?” is literally “Is your eye evil because I am good?” The evil eye is the jealous look that cannot bear another's good fortune.
vv: When those hired about five o’clock came, each of them received the usual daily wage.
The owner begins with the last, so that the first will see. The parable wants us to feel the shock.
Friend, I am doing you no wrong; did you not agree with me for the usual daily wage?
Justice is kept, and generosity goes beyond it. No one is wronged by grace given to another.
Or are you envious because I am generous?
ch: Many Fathers read the hours of the day as the ages of salvation history from Adam to Christ, and also as the stages of a human life, so that no one is called too late; so Origen and St Gregory the Great (in substance). The Catechism teaches that before God we have no strict right to merit, and that our merits are themselves gifts of his grace (CCC 2007, 2011).

qa: Is the owner unfair to the first workers?
No. They receive what was agreed. The parable is not a rule for wages but a picture of grace: eternal life is not earned by hours, but given by the Father's goodness, to the first and to the last.
study: Do I serve better when people are watching? What would it mean to work “so that the name of God may not be blasphemed”?
When does God's generosity to others make me grumble?

lead: On a Wednesday, a traditional fasting day in the Syriac Churches, the Gospel speaks of fasting and of the bridegroom. Ephesians shows what the bridegroom has done: he has broken down the dividing wall and built one household of God. The new wine of the Gospel needs a new people, joined together into a holy temple.

r.h: He is our peace
set: Ephesians 2 tells the story of salvation twice: from death to life (vv. 1–10), and from division to unity (vv. 11–22). The Gentile readers were once “far off”, strangers to the covenants of promise and without hope (2:12). Now in Christ they have been brought near.

In the Temple at Jerusalem a stone barrier separated the Court of the Gentiles from the inner courts, with inscriptions warning foreigners not to pass, on pain of death. Two of these stones, inscribed in Greek, have been found. Many interpreters think Paul has this wall in mind.
str: vv. 14–16: Christ is our peace: he made the two one, broke down the wall, created one new humanity, and reconciled both to God through the cross.
vv. 17–18: peace proclaimed to the far and the near; through him both have access in one Spirit to the Father.
vv. 19–22: no longer strangers but citizens and members of the household, a building growing into a holy temple.
kw: Literally “the middle wall”. Christ removed what separated Jews and Gentiles from each other, and both from God.
The right to be brought into the presence of a king. Notice the Trinity in v. 18: through Christ, in one Spirit, to the Father.
From Isaiah 28:16. The stone that holds the whole building together. The building stands because of Christ.
vv: For he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall, that is, the hostility between us.
Paul does not only say that Christ brings peace, but that he is our peace. Peace is a person.
So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God,
In him the whole structure is joined together and grows into a holy temple in the Lord;
The temple grows: it is alive. The renewal of the Church is growth, not only repair.
ch: The Second Vatican Council recalls this passage when it speaks of the Church's bond with the Jewish people: by his cross Christ our Peace reconciled Jews and Gentiles, making both one in himself (Nostra Aetate 4). The Catechism describes the Church as God's building, with Christ as the cornerstone and the faithful as living stones (CCC 756).

r.h: The bridegroom and the new wine
set: The disciples of John the Baptist, who fasted often, ask why Jesus' disciples do not. Devout Jews of the time fasted beyond what the Law required; the Pharisee in Luke's parable says, “I fast twice a week” (Luke 18:12). Jesus answers with three images: a wedding, a patch and wineskins.
str: v. 14: the question about fasting.
v. 15: the wedding guests cannot mourn while the bridegroom is with them; they will fast when he is taken away.
vv. 16–17: two short parables: unshrunk cloth on an old cloak, new wine in old skins.
kw: In the prophets God himself is Israel's bridegroom (Hosea 2:19; Isaiah 62:5). Jesus quietly takes the title for himself.
A goatskin used as a container. New wine is still fermenting and stretches the skin; an old, dry skin bursts.
vv: The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast.
An early hint of the Passion. Jesus does not abolish fasting; he changes its meaning. Christian fasting is longing for the bridegroom.
but new wine is put into fresh wineskins, and so both are preserved.
Matthew adds “and so both are preserved”, which Mark does not have. The new does not destroy what is good in the old; it needs a fitting vessel.
ch: The Didache, a Christian instruction from about the end of the first century, tells believers to fast on Wednesday and Friday (Didache 8). The Catechism names fasting, prayer and almsgiving as the chief forms of penance (CCC 1434).

rite: The Syriac tradition has long kept Wednesday and Friday as days of fasting, a custom already found in the Didache. Today's Gospel gives the reason: we fast because we long for the bridegroom, and we keep the fast with joy because he is risen.
study: Where do I still keep up a “dividing wall” against someone?
Is my fasting sad duty, or longing for the bridegroom?

lead: Paul prays that the eyes of the heart may be opened to see God's power at work in the risen Christ and in his Church. Mark's short parable shows the same power working in silence: the seed grows by itself, night and day, while the farmer sleeps. The Church grows by God's power, not by our anxiety.

r.h: The eyes of your heart enlightened
set: After the great blessing of 1:3–14, Paul gives thanks and prays for his readers. In Greek the prayer runs on as one long sentence. It moves from the readers' faith and love, to hope, inheritance and power, and ends with Christ raised, seated in heaven and given as head to the Church.
str: vv. 15–16: thanksgiving for their faith and love.
vv. 17–19: the prayer: a spirit of wisdom and revelation, and the eyes of the heart enlightened to know hope, inheritance and power.
vv. 20–23: that power shown in Christ: raised, seated above every power, head over all things for the Church, his body.
kw: In the Bible the heart is the centre of the person: thought, will and love. Faith gives the heart eyes.
The Church is “the fullness of him who fills all in all”: she is filled by Christ, and his fullness dwells in her for the world.
vv: so that, with the eyes of your heart enlightened, you may know what is the hope to which he has called you,
And he has put all things under his feet and has made him the head over all things for the church,
An echo of Psalm 8:6. The risen Christ is Lord of all creation, and he exercises his lordship for the good of the Church.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ is the head of the Body, and that the Church lives from him, in him and for him (CCC 792–795, in substance). The early Church called baptism itself “enlightenment”, because it opens the eyes of the heart (CCC 1216).

r.h: The seed grows by itself
set: This short parable is found only in Mark. It stands in the chapter of parables by the sea (Mark 4), after the sower and the lamp and before the mustard seed. Jesus' ministry looked small and met opposition; the parable says that God's Kingdom is already growing, though no one sees how.
str: v. 26: a man scatters seed.
v. 27: he sleeps and rises; the seed grows, he does not know how.
v. 28: the earth produces of itself: stalk, head, full grain.
v. 29: when the grain is ripe, the sickle and the harvest.
kw: The source of our word “automatic”. The growth comes from the seed and the soil, that is, from God, not from the farmer's effort.
The harvest image comes from Joel 3:13: “Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe.” Harvest is a biblical picture of the end of the age.
vv: and would sleep and rise night and day, and the seed would sprout and grow, he does not know how.
The farmer is not lazy; he has sown. But he cannot make the seed grow. This frees us from the anxiety of thinking that everything depends on us.
The earth produces of itself, first the stalk, then the head, then the full grain in the head.
Growth has stages. Patience belongs to faith.
ch: The Second Vatican Council compares the Kingdom to a seed: the word of the Lord, sown in the field, grows by its own power until the harvest (Lumen Gentium 5, in substance). The Church sows and trusts; the growth is God's.

study: What would I see differently if the “eyes of my heart” were enlightened?
Where must I sow and then trust, instead of trying to force the growth?

lead: Paul speaks of God's hidden wisdom, which no eye has seen and which the Spirit reveals. Jesus speaks of a treasure hidden in a field and a pearl of great value, worth everything we have. The Kingdom is hidden and must be found, and once found it changes everything. Today the Church remembers St John Chrysostom, the great preacher of Antioch.

r.h: God's wisdom, secret and hidden
set: Corinth prized eloquence and wisdom, and the church there was split into groups around favourite teachers (1:12). Paul has said that he came proclaiming “Christ crucified” (1:23), not with lofty words. Now he adds that there is a true wisdom, but it is God's, and only the Spirit reveals it.
str: vv. 6–8: a wisdom not of this age, hidden and decreed before the ages; the rulers did not understand it, or they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.
v. 9: what no eye has seen.
vv. 10–13: the Spirit searches the depths of God and teaches us.
vv. 14–15: the unspiritual person and the spiritual person.
kw: In v. 7 the NRSV renders it “secret”. In Paul a mystery is God's plan, once hidden and now revealed in Christ. The Syriac Churches call the sacraments raze, “mysteries”.
The psychikos lives by natural powers alone; the pneumatikos lives by the Spirit of God. It is not body against soul, but nature without grace against nature led by grace.
vv: None of the rulers of this age understood this; for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.
A startling title: the Crucified is the Lord of glory. The Fathers used this verse to show that the one who suffered is truly God, the Son made man.
What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the human heart conceived, what God has prepared for those who love him
The words are close to Isaiah 64:4 but are not an exact quotation; Paul may be joining texts. The Catechism uses them of the joy of heaven (CCC 1027).
these things God has revealed to us through the Spirit; for the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that to believe we need the grace of God and the inner help of the Holy Spirit, who moves the heart and opens the eyes of the mind (Dei Verbum 5). Faith is a gift of God (CCC 153).

r.h: The treasure, the pearl and the net
set: These are the last three of the seven parables of the Kingdom in Matthew 13, spoken to the disciples in the house (13:36). The treasure and the pearl belong together: both men sell all they have. The net, like the weeds among the wheat, speaks of the end of the age, when the good and the bad will be separated.
str: v. 44: the treasure hidden in a field.
vv. 45–46: the merchant and the one pearl.
vv. 47–50: the dragnet and the separation at the end.
vv. 51–52: “Have you understood all this?” and the scribe trained for the Kingdom.
kw: “In his joy he goes and sells all.” The selling is not a heavy loss; joy makes it light.
The scribe of v. 52 has been made a disciple for the Kingdom. He brings out both the new and the old: the Gospel and the Scriptures of Israel together.
vv: The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field, which someone found and hid; then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field.
on finding one pearl of great value, he went and sold all that he had and bought it.
The first man stumbles on the treasure; the merchant searches for it. God is found in both ways.
Therefore every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven is like the master of a household who brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old.
Many see here a portrait of Matthew himself, and of every good teacher in the Church.
ch: The Catechism quotes these parables: to gain the Kingdom one must give everything (CCC 546). On v. 52 the Council recalls St Augustine's rule: the New Testament lies hidden in the Old, and the Old is made plain in the New (Dei Verbum 16).

rite: St John Chrysostom (about 349–407), priest of Antioch and later Archbishop of Constantinople, is one of the greatest preachers of the Church; his name means “golden-mouthed”. Antioch is the mother city of the West Syriac tradition to which the Syro-Malankara Church belongs. In Malayalam he is called Mar Ivanios, a form of the name John. The same name was taken by Archbishop Geevarghese Mar Ivanios, who led the reunion of the Malankara Catholic Church with Rome in 1930.
study: What is the “treasure” for which I would gladly sell everything? Does my life show it?
How do the Old and New Testaments help each other in my reading of Scripture?

lead: On the feast of St Philip the Apostle, Paul describes the apostles as servants of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries, judged by the Lord alone. In the Gospel Philip says, “Lord, show us the Father,” and Jesus answers, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” The steward's whole task is to show Christ, and in Christ the Father.

r.h: Stewards of God's mysteries
set: The Corinthians compared their teachers, Paul, Apollos and Cephas, and took sides (1:12; 3:4–5). Paul ends this section by telling them how to think of their ministers: not as heads of parties, but as servants and stewards who must answer to the Lord.
str: v. 1: servants of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries.
v. 2: what is required of stewards: trustworthiness.
vv. 3–4: Paul does not even judge himself; the Lord judges.
v. 5: do not judge before the time; the Lord will bring to light what is hidden.
kw: The manager of a household, often himself a slave, who gives out what belongs to the master. The steward distributes what is not his own.
The one quality required. Not brilliance, but faithfulness.
vv: Think of us in this way, as servants of Christ and stewards of God’s mysteries.
Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found trustworthy.
Therefore do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart.
Only God sees the heart. This frees ministers both from pride and from the fear of human opinion.
ch: The Church applies this text above all to bishops and priests, who administer the sacraments, the mysteries of God, and must be found faithful. Every baptized person is also a steward, called to use each gift received “like good stewards of the manifold grace of God” (1 Peter 4:10).

r.h: Whoever has seen me has seen the Father
set: The scene is the Last Supper, in Jesus' farewell discourse (John 13–17). Jesus has just said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (14:6). Thomas asked about the way; now Philip asks to see the Father.

Philip came from Bethsaida, the town of Andrew and Peter (1:44). In John he brings Nathanael to Jesus (1:45), is tested by Jesus before the feeding of the five thousand (6:5–7), and brings the Greeks who wish to see Jesus (12:21–22). He is a practical and honest man.
str: v. 7: to know Jesus is to know the Father.
v. 8: Philip's request.
vv. 9–11: whoever has seen me has seen the Father; I am in the Father and the Father in me.
v. 12: believers will do greater works.
vv. 13–14: whatever you ask in my name.
kw: Philip's prayer echoes Moses: “Show me your glory, I pray” (Exodus 33:18). What Moses could not see, the disciples see in the face of Jesus.
To ask in Jesus' name is to ask as one united to him, according to his will, for the glory of the Father.
vv: Lord, show us the Father, and we will be satisfied.
Philip asks for the one thing that would satisfy the human heart. Jesus tells him he has had it all along.
Have I been with you all this time, Philip, and you still do not know me? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.
A gentle reproach, by name. Jesus is not a messenger pointing beyond himself; he is the image of the Father.
I will do whatever you ask in my name, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ's whole life is a revelation of the Father, and cites this verse (CCC 516). The Fathers used John 14:9–10 to show that the Son is one in being with the Father, as the Council of Nicaea confessed (in substance). Prayer in the name of Jesus is the heart of Christian prayer (CCC 2614, 2664–2666).

rite: St Philip the Apostle is remembered today in the Syro-Malankara calendar; the Latin Church keeps his feast with St James on 3 May. An early tradition, recorded by Eusebius, says that Philip was buried at Hierapolis in Asia Minor. His request is the prayer of every seeker, and Jesus' answer is fulfilled at every Holy Qurbono: in the Son we see the Father.
study: What do I ask God to “show” me before I will be satisfied?
How can I be a faithful steward of what I have received, in my family and parish?

lead: Today the Syro-Malankara Church begins the season of Suboro, the “good news” or Annunciation. The first good news of the New Testament is not given in Nazareth but in the Temple of Jerusalem, to an old priest at the hour of incense. The Evening Gospel (Luke 1:1–17) already opens the scene with Luke's preface and the angel's promise.

The four Old Testament lessons all speak of God at work where human hope has run out. Sarah, too old to bear, is promised Isaac (Genesis 17). Ruth the Moabite binds herself to Naomi and to Naomi's God (Ruth 1). Hannah, barren and mocked, pours out her soul at the sanctuary (1 Samuel 1). Isaiah hears God say to a weak people, “Do not fear, for I am with you” (Isaiah 41). The Catholic Epistle (2 Peter 1:3–11) reminds us that God's promises make us “participants of the divine nature”.

We study three readings closely: Genesis 17:15–22, the Old Testament lesson that stands closest to the Gospel and to the Epistle; Romans 4:13–25, where Paul reads that same story as the school of faith; and Luke 1:5–25, the message to Zechariah. The key words are promise, barrenness and believing.

r.h: A son for Abraham and Sarah
set: Genesis 17 is the chapter of the covenant of circumcision. Abraham is ninety-nine years old (17:1). God changes his name from Abram to Abraham, “father of a multitude” (17:5), and gives circumcision as the sign of the covenant (17:9–14).

Ishmael, Abraham's son by Hagar, is already thirteen (17:25), and Abraham seems to have settled on him as his heir. Today's verses make the promise sharper than ever before: the son of the promise will come from Sarah herself. Chapter 18 tells the same promise again, heard this time by Sarah at the tent door, where she too laughs (18:12) and the Lord asks, “Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?” (18:14).
str: vv. 15–16: Sarai becomes Sarah; she will be blessed and will be the mother of nations and kings.
v. 17: Abraham falls on his face and laughs.
v. 18: his plea for Ishmael.
vv. 19–21: God's answer: a son from Sarah, named Isaac, the heir of the everlasting covenant; Ishmael too will be blessed.
v. 22: God goes up from Abraham.

¶ The passage has the shape of an annunciation: God appears, gives a message, meets an objection, names the child and fixes the time. Luke's two annunciations, to Zechariah and to Mary, follow the same pattern.
kw: Both Sarai and Sarah are usually understood as forms of the word for “princess”. The new name marks a new mission: kings will come from her (17:16). In the Bible a new name means a new vocation.
The child's name plays on Abraham's laughter (17:17). Later Sarah says, “God has brought laughter for me” (21:6). The laugh of doubt becomes the laugh of joy.
The covenant does not depend on Abraham's strength or age. God binds himself to it for all generations (17:19).
vv: Then Abraham fell on his face and laughed, and said to himself, “Can a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old? Can Sarah, who is ninety years old, bear a child?”
Two gestures together: Abraham bows in worship and laughs in disbelief. God does not reject him. He takes the laugh and turns it into the child's name.
God said, “No, but your wife Sarah shall bear you a son, and you shall name him Isaac.
God's “No” to Abraham's smaller hope is a “Yes” to something greater than he dared to ask. Many unanswered prayers are of this kind.
As for Ishmael, I have heard you; I will bless him and make him fruitful and exceedingly numerous;
The name Ishmael means “God hears” (16:11). Even when God chooses another path, he hears the father's prayer for his son.
ch: The New Testament reads Sarah's motherhood as the fruit of faith (Romans 4:19; Hebrews 11:11). The Catechism names Sarah among the holy women of the Old Covenant whose mission prepared for that of Mary: against all human expectation God chooses those who seemed powerless, to show his faithfulness to his promises (CCC 489). The angel's word to Mary, “nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37), is the answer to the question asked at Abraham's tent.

r.h: Abraham hoped against hope
set: In Romans 1–3 Paul shows that all, Jews and Gentiles alike, need God's saving justice, and that it is given as a gift through faith in Christ (3:21–26). Chapter 4 brings Abraham as the proof from Scripture: “he believed the Lord; and the Lord reckoned it to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6).
In 4:9–12 Paul has noted that Abraham was counted righteous in Genesis 15, before he was circumcised in Genesis 17. So Abraham is the father both of the circumcised and of the Gentiles who believe.
str: vv. 13–15: the promise did not come through the law.
vv. 16–17: it rests on faith so that it may be grace, for all Abraham's children.
vv. 18–21: a portrait of Abraham's faith before an old body and a barren womb.
v. 22: therefore it was reckoned to him as righteousness.
vv. 23–25: the same is written for us who believe in the God who raised Jesus.
kw: The key word of the chapter. A promise depends on the one who makes it. That is why it can rest on grace (v. 16).

A word from accounting, used again and again in this chapter. God enters faith into the account as righteousness. The Church understands this not as a mere label but as a real gift that makes us just (CCC 1992).
Literally “beyond hope, upon hope” (v. 18). Every human reason for hope had gone; Abraham rested on God's word.
vv: in the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist.
Two titles of God: he raises the dead and he creates from nothing. Abraham's “dead” body, Sarah's barren womb and the tomb of Jesus are three places where this God has acted.
Hoping against hope, he believed that he would become “the father of many nations,”
He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was already as good as dead (for he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah’s womb.

A note on the text. Many later manuscripts read “he did not consider his own body”, as in older English Bibles. The oldest manuscripts, followed by the NRSV and the POC, say that he did consider it. Faith here does not close its eyes to the facts; it looks at them squarely and still trusts God.
who was handed over to death for our trespasses and was raised for our justification.
The words “handed over” echo the Greek of the Servant song (Isaiah 53:12). The Resurrection is not only proof of salvation; it belongs to salvation itself.
ch: The Catechism presents Abraham as the model of the obedience of faith and quotes Paul: “hoping against hope” he believed (CCC 145–146). It cites Romans 4:25 to teach that the Paschal mystery has two sides: by his death Christ delivers us from sin, and by his Resurrection he opens the way to new life, which is above all justification (CCC 654). The Council of Trent called faith “the beginning of human salvation, the foundation and root of all justification” (Session 6, chapter 8). Catholics and Lutherans set out their shared understanding of this teaching in the Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999).

r.h: The message to Zechariah in the Temple
set: Luke opens with a careful Greek preface for Theophilus (1:1–4, read at the Evening Gospel), then changes style and tells the story in the language of the Greek Old Testament. “King Herod of Judea” is Herod the Great, who died in 4 BC.

The priests were divided into twenty-four courses (1 Chronicles 24); the course of Abijah was the eighth (24:10). Each course served in the Temple for a week, twice a year. Incense was offered every morning and evening on the golden altar inside the Holy Place, and the priest was chosen by lot. Later Jewish tradition (the Mishnah) says that only priests who had never offered incense took part in that lot, so for Zechariah this was the hour of his life.
In that culture childlessness was felt as a public disgrace (1:25). Luke insists that it was not a punishment: both were “righteous before God” (1:6).
str: vv. 5–7: a righteous, childless, aging couple.
vv. 8–10: the hour of incense; the people pray outside.
vv. 11–17: the angel and the message: a son named John, the forerunner with the spirit of Elijah.
vv. 18–20: Zechariah's question and the sign of silence.
vv. 21–23: the waiting people and the mute priest.
vv. 24–25: Elizabeth conceives.
¶ Luke sets this scene beside the annunciation to Mary (1:26–38): the Temple and a village, an old priest and a young woman, a question of doubt and a question of faith.
kw: “the Lord remembered” / “the Lord has shown favour”
The names tell the story: God remembers, and God gives grace. Elizabeth's name is that of Aaron's wife, Elisheba (Exodus 6:23): this is a wholly priestly family.
The angel who came to Daniel “at the time of the evening sacrifice” (Daniel 9:21) comes again at the hour of incense. The time of fulfilment has arrived.
Luke's first use of the verb of the Gospel (1:19). The Syriac name of the season, Suboro, carries the same meaning: the message, the good news.
vv: But the angel said to him, “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard. Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you will name him John.
Which prayer? Perhaps the old prayer for a child, which he may have stopped praying; perhaps the priest's prayer for the redemption of Israel. In John both are answered at once.
With the spirit and power of Elijah he will go before him, to turn the hearts of parents to their children,
The angel quotes Malachi 4:5–6, the last words of the prophets in our Old Testament. “Before him” means before the Lord God (v. 16). As the Gospel unfolds, the Lord whom John precedes is Jesus.
But now, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time, you will become mute, unable to speak, until the day these things occur.

The silence is both discipline and sign. When the child is named, Zechariah's mouth is opened and his first words are praise (1:64). The priest who could not bless the waiting people (v. 22) foreshadows the end of the Gospel, where Jesus lifts up his hands and blesses his disciples, who return to the Temple praising God (24:50–53).
ch: The Catechism calls John the Lord's immediate precursor, sent to prepare his way, “more than a prophet” (CCC 523), and teaches that in him the Holy Spirit completes the preparation of the people for the Lord; he was filled with the Spirit even from his mother's womb (CCC 717–718). St Ambrose, commenting on Luke, praises Zechariah and Elizabeth as righteous in both priestly and married life (in substance). St Ephrem contrasts the priest who doubted and was made silent with the Virgin who believed and conceived the Word (in substance).
